messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 53
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Painter
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 34

He is 53 years old and speaks about the war years in a measured, careful way, as though keeping the details in order is one way of keeping them contained. Before the violence, he lives a plain, working life as a painter, moving from building to building with his brushes, ladders, and tins of color. He takes pride in making tired walls look clean again. He knows how to cover damage. That becomes part of why the war is so difficult for him: everywhere he looks, there is damage that cannot be painted over.

When fighting reaches his city, the ordinary rhythm of his life breaks apart. He remembers the first days of shelling as unreal, as if the noise belongs to someone else’s neighborhood. Then the sounds come closer. Streets empty. Shops close. Clients stop calling. He continues working when he can, partly to earn money and partly to give the day some shape, but each outing requires more calculation. He learns which roads are safer, which hours to avoid, which walls tremble when an explosion lands nearby. He becomes alert in a way that never fully turns off. Even at home with his wife, he listens for distant blasts and the tone of people’s footsteps in the stairwell.

One incident stays with him most. He is outside with his tools when violence erupts unexpectedly nearby. He cannot remember every detail in a clean sequence, only the immediacy of needing to get low, to protect his head, to find cover while people scream and run. Afterwards, he notices a strange silence in his body, a coldness that comes over him before fear does. He later describes the scene in fragments: dust in his mouth, a smell of burning, his heart striking hard enough to make him feel sick. The image that returns most often is not a face but the moment of not knowing whether the next sound will be the one that kills him.

After that, he begins to live differently. He avoids the roads, buildings, and open spaces that remind him of the attack. He measures every day by danger. He starts scanning rooftops and windows almost automatically, and he feels exposed even in places that should be safe. When a motorbike backfires, his whole body jerks before he can think. Sudden sounds leave him angry and shaken. He says his nerves feel “pulled tight,” and that is how he moves through his home, with tension in his shoulders and jaw as if he is bracing against impact.

Sleep becomes broken and unreliable. He falls asleep late because he cannot settle, and when he does sleep, he wakes with his heart racing from dreams he cannot fully explain. Some nights he wakes with the sense that he has heard something, and he checks the doors and windows repeatedly. His wife urges him back to bed, but he stands in the dark, listening. He does not like that he has become so watchful, but he also cannot stop. He feels responsible for keeping his family safe, and that responsibility has become heavy and constant.

As the fighting eventually lessens, he remains changed. He returns to painting, but even that work now carries reminders. The smell of thinner can bring him back to days when he was trying to work under threat. A sudden bang from a dropped ladder can leave him pale and angry with himself for flinching. He still completes jobs, still speaks politely to clients, but he uses more energy than before to maintain his composure. At home, he is quieter. He loves his wife and adult children, yet he often feels distant from them, as though some part of him is still standing in the war zone, listening for the next explosion.

He describes guilt in a restrained way, not as dramatic remorse but as an uneasy question that follows him: why did he survive when others did not, why did he keep working when so many things were collapsing around him, why can’t he simply be grateful to be alive? He tries to push these thoughts aside, yet they return in quiet moments, especially when he is alone in the evening. He stays busy to avoid them, fills his time with chores, repairs, and work calls. Still, there are moments when he sits motionless, staring at a wall he has painted and feeling that the color looks the same as before, but his life does not.
